name: How to Fix Broken Links and Server Errors That Hurt My Visibility

step.name: Step 1: Conduct a Comprehensive Site Crawl
step.text: The very first thing you need to do is get a clear picture of all the broken links, redirect chains, and server errors on your site. Use a reliable site crawler tool (there are many free and paid options available) to simulate how a search engine bot navigates your site. This tool will identify all the URLs that return a 4xx (client error, like 'page not found') or 5xx (server error) status code, as well as any excessively long redirect chains. It's essential to not just check your primary pages, but every single link, including those to images, CSS, and JavaScript files, as these can also cause crawlability issues if they're broken. A thorough crawl gives you the data you need to prioritize fixes.

step.name: Step 2: Prioritize and Fix Broken Internal Links
step.text: Once you have your crawl report, focus on broken internal links first. These are links within your own website that point to pages that no longer exist or are returning errors. Fixing these is crucial because they directly impact user experience and prevent crawlers from efficiently moving through your site's architecture. For each broken internal link, either update the link to point to a correct, existing page, or remove the link if the content is truly gone. For pages that have moved, implement proper 301 redirects to guide both users and search engines to the new location. Avoid creating redirect chains (multiple redirects from one URL to another to another) as these slow down crawlers and dilute link equity.

step.name: Step 3: Address Server Errors (5xx status codes)
step.text: Server errors (like 500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable) indicate a problem with your web server itself, preventing your site from delivering content. These are critical issues that must be resolved immediately, as they can cause significant drops in rankings and completely block search engine access. Work with your hosting provider or development team to diagnose and fix the root cause of these errors. Common causes include misconfigured server settings, database problems, or overloaded servers. Monitoring your server logs can help identify recurring issues. Ensuring your server reliably returns an HTTP 200 status for all accessible pages is non-negotiable for crawlability.

step.name: Step 4: Update Your XML Sitemaps and Request Recrawls
step.text: After fixing broken links and server errors, update your XML sitemaps to reflect these changes. Remove any URLs that no longer exist and ensure all newly corrected or moved pages are included. Submit the updated sitemap through Google Search Console. Additionally, for critical pages that were previously affected by errors, use the URL Inspection tool in Search Console to request a recrawl. While this doesn't guarantee instant indexing, it signals to Google that these pages need attention. This step ensures that search engines are aware of your fixes and can more quickly process the corrected information, helping to restore your visibility.
